lines.text: to abandon them in the name of God; and then it is not that
he wants to abandon house and home, wife and child, he
would rather cling to them so long as God permits and serve
God thereby, yet he is also ready for resignation when God
wills to take them from him." To-day we are all involved in
a situation in which we must be prepared for God to take
away from us what He gave, and for many of our friends and
relations this has already happened. How stands it with us?
Are we resigned to God's will?
We may also be tempted to conceal our essential poverty
by the wealth of our mind and moral dispositions, by the
consciousness of what we are able to achieve, in fact by the
consciousness of our courageous readiness for self-sacrifice;
by the pride which trusts in one's own strength of will and
moral resources, by the sense of security which a man wins
through purposeful work and devotion to those values which
lend to a human life dignity and distinction. But has such
pride, such self-security, any longer its convincing power in
these days when our world, in which we dwelt with a sense of
pride and security, is falling into ruins before our eyes? Does
not such an attitude now stand out as the arrogance of man
who forgets that he is poor, that he is futile?
"Blessed are the poor in spirit"—the word is intended to
comfort the poor who realize their poverty. But it does not
comfort them by reinterpreting their poverty as riches; it
does not mean: in the awareness of your poverty resides your
wealth! There is an attitude of spiritual superiority which
derives from the consciousness of penetrating the essential
vanity of all things; there is a spirit of sceptical irony which
looks with a scornful compassion on the busy and tumultuous
affairs of men; there is a condescending type of humour
which surveys the bustle of the human scene with cold
detachment. It is true that of all human attitudes such irony
and humour stand nearest to the Christian faith. But the
spiritually poor are not they who from a safe distance
ironically or humorously contemplate the course of events;
for in such an attitude there still lurks the pride of man who
